meta.name: Sourdough Bread - 70% Hydration
meta.description: A beginner-friendly overnight sourdough recipe yielding two boules. Four ingredients, 70% hydration, stretch-and-fold method, overnight room-temperature bulk ferment, cold proof, sequential Dutch oven bake. Optimized for simplicity without sacrificing quality.

states.title: Prepare Workspace
states.direction: Gather all vessels, equipment, and ingredients. Weigh out bread flour, water, starter, and salt into separate containers.
states.exit_condition: All ingredients weighed, vessels and equipment laid out

notes.text: Starter must be active and bubbly — should have doubled within 4-8 hours of its last feeding
If starter hasn't doubled, add 1/8 tsp instant yeast to the dough as insurance — King Arthur and The Perfect Loaf both endorse this

states.title: Combine Flour, Water & Starter
states.direction: In the large mixing bowl (V1), combine 700g water (or 675g, holding back 25g for salt incorporation) and 200g active starter. Stir to dissolve. Add 1000g bread flour. Mix with a fork or spatula until no dry flour remains — a shaggy, rough mass. Do NOT add salt yet.
states.exit_condition: Flour, water, and starter combined into a shaggy mass with no dry flour visible. Salt NOT added yet.

notes.text: Do not knead. Just stir until combined. Gluten will develop through stretch-and-fold and time.

Fermentolyse = mixing flour, water, and starter WITHOUT salt, then resting before adding salt. Delayed salt addition allows gluten to begin developing uninhibited. Confirmed across multiple bakes — dough is noticeably stronger at first stretch and fold compared to mixing everything at once.

states.title: Rest
states.direction: Cover the bowl and let the dough rest for 30 minutes at room temperature. The flour hydrates and gluten begins developing without salt inhibiting the process.
states.exit_condition: 30 minutes elapsed, dough relaxed and slightly cohesive

states.title: Add Salt & Incorporate
states.direction: Sprinkle 20g fine sea salt over the dough. If you held back 25g water, pour it over the salt. Fold the dough over itself several times to incorporate the salt — squeeze, fold, and press until no salt granules remain.
states.exit_condition: Salt fully incorporated, no granules felt when pressing dough

notes.text: The reserved water helps dissolve and distribute the salt evenly. If you used all 700g water in the fermentolyse, just fold the salt in dry — it works fine.

reminders.prompt: Take aliquot sample after incorporating salt

states.title: Stretch & Fold — Set 1
states.direction: With a wet hand, grab the north side of the dough, stretch it up as far as it will go without tearing, and fold it over the center. Rotate the bowl 90 degrees and repeat for all 4 sides (north, east, south, west). Cover.
states.exit_condition: All 4 sides stretched and folded, dough is in a rough package

notes.text: Wet your hand first to prevent sticking — do not flour

Target aliquot rise depends on the average dough temperature across the entire bulk ferment. Warmer dough cuts off earlier because it keeps fermenting through shaping and cold retard. These are low-end targets — start here and calibrate up 10% if underproofed. At 80°F and warmer, supplement with a full dough-strength check, not just % rise.

table.caption: Bulk fermentation guidelines — target rise by average dough temp

states.title: Rest
states.direction: Cover the bowl and let the dough rest for 30 minutes at room temperature.
states.exit_condition: 30 minutes elapsed

states.title: Stretch & Fold — Set 2
states.direction: Repeat stretch and fold: wet hand, grab one side, stretch up, fold over center. All 4 sides. Cover.
states.exit_condition: All 4 sides stretched and folded, dough feels slightly stronger and smoother

states.title: Rest
states.direction: Cover the bowl and let the dough rest for 30 minutes at room temperature.
states.exit_condition: 30 minutes elapsed

states.title: Stretch & Fold — Set 3
states.direction: Final stretch and fold: wet hand, all 4 sides. The dough should now feel noticeably smoother and more elastic than the first set. Cover tightly with plastic wrap.
states.exit_condition: Dough is smooth and elastic, covered tightly for overnight bulk

notes.text: 3 is standard — 4th optional if dough feels under-developed. This is 90 seconds of total work.

states.title: Overnight Bulk Ferment
states.direction: Leave the covered bowl on the counter at room temperature (70-74°F / 21-23°C) overnight (10-12 hours). Do not use the oven with light on — it runs too warm. The dough ferments while you sleep.
states.exit_condition: Dough has increased 50-75% in volume (NOT doubled), surface is domed with visible bubbles, jiggles when bowl is shaken. If dough has doubled or is flat/slack, it is over-fermented — shape immediately or pivot to focaccia.

notes.text: Watch the dough, not the clock. Use the aliquot jar to track rise % — visual cues and measured rise matter more than time. At 75°F (24°C) bulk takes ~8 hours. At 65°F (18°C) it could take 12+ hours.

If dough has more than doubled and looks very puffy with large bubbles, it is over-fermented. Shape immediately and bake sooner. If dough tears during shaping, pivot to focaccia: flatten into an oiled dish, top with olive oil, herbs, salt, and parmesan. Bake at 425°F (220°C) for ~40 min.

Do NOT use oven with light on for bulk ferment — oven light runs 78-90°F+, far too warm for 20% inoculation. Counter at 70-74°F is ideal. Two bakes over-fermented using oven light before switching to counter.
If over-fermentation recurs with the doubled batch, consider reducing starter to 15% (150g) or 10% (100g) for a wider overnight window. Lower inoculation also develops more complex sour flavor.
Aliquot targets by dough temperature: ~30% rise at 80°F+ (27°C+), ~40-50% at 75-79°F (24-26°C), ~50-60% at 70-74°F (21-23°C). Warmer dough ferments faster — adjust target down to avoid over-proofing.

states.title: Turn Out Dough
states.direction: Lightly flour the counter. Gently scrape the fermented dough out of the bowl onto the floured surface. Sprinkle a light dusting of flour on top of the dough.
states.exit_condition: Dough is on the floured counter, right-side up

states.title: Divide Dough
states.direction: Using a bench scraper, divide the dough in half — each piece should be roughly 960g. Don't fuss over exact weight. Use the bench scraper in one decisive motion; avoid sawing.
states.exit_condition: Two roughly equal dough pieces (~960g each) on the counter

notes.text: Weigh both pieces — uneven loaves bake unevenly. Target ~960g per piece for a 2-loaf bake.

states.title: Pre-Shape
states.direction: Using a bench scraper, gently form each piece into a loose round — tuck the edges under to create a rough ball. Don't worry about perfection. The goal is a general round shape with some surface tension. Repeat for both pieces.
states.exit_condition: Both pieces are in loose round shapes on the counter

notes.text: Pre-shaping relaxes the gluten before final shaping, making it much easier to build tension in the envelope fold. Standard practice for every bake.

states.title: Bench Rest
states.direction: Leave both pre-shaped rounds uncovered on the counter for 15-20 minutes. The gluten relaxes, making final shaping easier.
states.exit_condition: Both rounds have rested 15-20 minutes, slightly spread but still holding general shape

states.title: Envelope Fold
states.direction: One piece at a time: flip the dough over so the sticky side faces up. Fold like an envelope: bottom edge up to center, left side over to center, right side over to center, top edge down to center. Flip the whole package seam-side down onto a clean, UNFLOURED section of counter. Repeat for the second piece.
states.exit_condition: Both pieces are folded into rough rounds, seam-side down on unfloured surface

states.title: Build Surface Tension
states.direction: One piece at a time: cup your hands around the dough (palms don't touch the top). Gently drag it toward you in a short motion — the bottom grips the unfloured surface and tucks under, creating tension on top. Rotate a quarter turn. Repeat 4-6 times until the top is smooth and taut, like a stretched balloon. Repeat for the second piece.
states.exit_condition: Both pieces have smooth, taut, rounded surfaces with visible surface tension

notes.text: The unfloured counter is intentional — friction between the dough and counter creates the tension. Do not flour here.
If the dough tears, stop. Let it rest 5 minutes and try again with fewer, gentler drags.

states.title: Into Proofing Basket
states.direction: Dust both proofing baskets (V2a, V2b) generously with rice flour — flour the banneton directly, no linen liner. Using a bench scraper, lift each shaped dough and place seam-side UP into a basket. If seams have opened, pinch closed. Cover both with plastic wrap.
states.exit_condition: Both loaves are seam-side up in floured bannetons (no linen), covered with plastic wrap

notes.text: Rice flour is best for dusting — it's gluten-free so it won't stick to the dough. Regular flour works but rice flour is more reliable.
Flour banneton directly (no linen liner) — confirmed better blistering and release across multiple bakes. Towel-lined bowl works as a backup.

states.title: Room Temperature Rest
states.direction: Leave both covered baskets on the counter at room temperature for approximately 1 hour. The dough settles into the banneton and begins its final rise before cold proofing.
states.exit_condition: ~1 hour at room temperature, dough has settled in banneton

notes.text: Allows the dough to settle before building final tension with a stitch. Standard practice.

states.title: Stitch for Tension
states.direction: One banneton at a time: with wet fingers, pull opposite edges of the dough toward the center in an overlapping pattern — like lacing a shoe. Work around the top of the dough, pulling each side to the center and pressing gently. This rebuilds surface tension after the room-temp rest. Repeat for the second banneton.
states.exit_condition: Dough surface is taut in both bannetons, stitched edges visible on top (this becomes the bottom when turned out)

notes.text: Stitching adds tension without deflating the dough. Bakes that included stitching before cold proof showed better shape retention during scoring and loading.

states.title: Cold Proof in Fridge
states.direction: Place both covered baskets in the refrigerator. Cold proof for 1-24 hours. The fridge slows fermentation, develops flavor, and makes the dough easier to score.
states.exit_condition: Both loaves have been in fridge at least 1 hour (up to 24 hours). Begin preheating oven when ready to bake.

notes.text: The fridge is your pause button. Shaped dough can sit 1-48 hours. Bake whenever it's convenient.
Longer cold proof = more tangy, complex flavor. 12-18 hours is the sweet spot for overnight.

reminders.prompt: Note fridge entry time for cold proof tracking

states.title: Preheat Oven + Dutch Oven
states.direction: Place the Dutch oven with lid (V3) on the middle rack. Preheat to 500°F (260°C) for at least 60 minutes. The heavy pot needs time to fully saturate with heat.
states.exit_condition: Oven at 500°F (260°C) for at least 60 minutes, Dutch oven fully preheated

notes.text: Start preheating while the dough is still in the fridge. Do NOT let the dough warm up — bake straight from cold.

states.title: Score the Dough
states.direction: Remove the first loaf from fridge (leave the second in the fridge). Turn out onto a sheet of parchment paper (it will release from the floured banneton). Using a bread lame or sharp knife, score a cross (X) pattern across the top — two perpendicular cuts about 1 cm deep. Use swift, confident strokes.
states.exit_condition: First loaf scored with clean X pattern on parchment paper, ready for Dutch oven

notes.text: Score the dough cold — cold dough is firm and scores cleanly. Warm dough drags and tears.
Hold the blade at 90 degrees (straight down) for a boule. Deeper than you think — about 1 cm.
Use parchment paper as scoring and loading surface — score directly on parchment, then use it as a sling to lower into Dutch oven. Silicone slings cause sticking.
Cross score for production bakes — consistent spring, good ear, uniform look. Single score and decorative patterns add risk without payoff on this dough.

states.title: Bake — Covered
states.direction: Carefully remove the preheated Dutch oven. Lower the first scored loaf into the pot using the parchment as a sling. Cover with the lid. Return to oven. Reduce temperature to 450°F (230°C). Bake covered for 20 minutes.
states.exit_condition: 20 minutes elapsed with lid on

notes.text: The lid traps steam from the dough, keeping the crust pliable for maximum oven spring and creating a glossy, blistered crust
Be extremely careful — the Dutch oven is 500°F. Use oven mitts and move deliberately.

For 2-loaf bakes: after the first loaf finishes, re-preheat oven to 500°F (260°C) for 30 minutes before loading the second loaf. Second loaf may need rotating or flipping at ~15 minutes for even browning.

states.title: Bake — Uncovered
states.direction: Remove the lid from the Dutch oven. Reduce temperature to 425-450°F (218-232°C). Bake uncovered 9 minutes, flip the loaf for even browning, bake another 9 minutes. Gauge by look and feel — pull when the crust is deep golden brown and crackling. Transfer to cooling rack. Score the second loaf (from fridge), load into the still-hot Dutch oven, and repeat the covered + uncovered bake.
states.exit_condition: Both loaves baked — deep golden brown crust, hollow sound when tapped, internal temp 210°F (99°C)

notes.text: Don't pull it early because it looks dark — a deep brown crust has the best flavor and crunch. Pale = undercooked.

reminders.prompt: (Optional) Record internal temperature out of oven (target 210°F / 99°C)

states.title: Cool on Rack
states.direction: Place both loaves on a wire rack. The first loaf gets extra cooling time while the second bakes. Let each loaf cool for at least 1 hour before slicing. The bread is still cooking internally as it cools.
states.exit_condition: Bread has cooled at least 1 hour, no longer hot to the touch

notes.text: Cutting too early = gummy interior. The starches are still setting as the bread cools. This is the hardest part — resist the urge.
You'll hear the crust crackling as it cools. That's normal — it's called "singing" and means the crust is crisping up.

reminders.prompt: Rate crust: color, ear development, blistering

cook_log.summary: First 100% Marquis (BSM) sub for the 70% formula. Sluggish starter, 60min autolyse, three folds, 64% aliquot, double-shaping loaf 2 to fix surface tension. Loaf 1 baked with Dutch oven lid not fully closed — steam loss, poor spring, dense crumb, complex but acetic-forward flavor. Loaf 2 experimental step-down uncovered (450→425→350); couldn't hit Tartine's 412°F internal target. Bread is bread, even if it's just a frisbee.
notes: First bake using Barton Springs Mill Marquis — 100% sub for the 1000g bread flour. Bag was just over 1kg so weighed out exactly 1000g.
Starter was sluggish before mix — didn't pass float test. Smelled fine, not vinegar. Had used Ryman Rye in starter, effectively making it the levain.
Autolyse extended to 60min for the stone-ground whole-grain flour (BSM house rule).
Mix: 1000g Marquis, 700g water (70%), 200g starter, 20g salt. Dough 79.3°F after autolyse, 80.1°F after salt + fold 1.
Three folds at 12:00pm, 12:38pm, 1:19pm. Dough cooled to ~78°F by fold 2 and held.
Bulk monitored via aliquot: 0% at salt-in (noon), 30% at 2:19pm, 64% at 3:30pm → preshape go.
Yield post-bulk 1893g (≈27g bowl loss from 1920g formula). Target 946g per loaf.
Loaf 1 shaped at 4:39pm (940g). Loaf 2 surface tension not satisfying — bench rested another 20min, shaped at 5:12pm (954g).
Both loaves into fridge for overnight cold retard.
Loaf 1 bake: preheated Dutch oven 490°F/60min, covered 450°F/20min, uncovered 425°F/20min. Internal ~208°F, hollow knock, no crackling (probably from lack of spring).
Notable issue: didn't notice Dutch oven lid wasn't fully closed during covered phase — steam not trapped. Morning brain + poor kitchen light.
Loaf 2 out of fridge around 7:14am (when loaf 1's covered bake started). Cold retard ~14hr.

Loaf 2 bake: preheat #2 500°F/30min, covered 450°F/20min, then Tartine-style uncovered 450°F/20min, then stepped down 425°F/5min, then 350°F/5min for browning. Total 30min uncovered. Still couldn't hit Tartine's 412°F internal target — possibly thermometer dwell or pulled too early.

Loaf 1 assessment: flavor complex (not just sour), acetic-forward — more sour than usual. Crumb dense as expected for heritage stone-ground. Spring poor — self-diagnosed impatient shaping + the lid-not-closed steam loss. 'Bread is bread, even if it's just a frisbee.' Loaf 2 given away — no taste data.

Both loaves bagged in kraft paper bread bags with windowed fronts showing the banneton spiral crusts. 'Especially for you — thank you' kraft seal stickers in the foreground waiting to be applied. Loaf 2 heading out as a gift.

next_time.text: Bump hydration to 80% for whole-grain Marquis — Tartine's whole-wheat spec. 70% gives dense crumb on heritage stone-ground flour.

Possibly skip overnight cold retard — whole-wheat ferments faster than bread flour, so long retard amplifies acetic sour beyond preference. Try shorter (4-6hr) or skip.

Predicted disaster from the flour mistake → best oven spring on a regular sourdough in a while. Working theory: AP/rice blend swap removed whole-wheat bran, leaving more intact gluten + rice flour acting as steam-release starch filler.

techniques.name: 3 stretch-and-fold sets
techniques.sourcedFrom: The Fresh Loaf, Foodbod, The Perfect Loaf
techniques.rationale: Diminishing returns above 3-4 sets. 90 seconds total investment for major structural improvement.

techniques.name: Overnight room-temp bulk ferment
techniques.sourcedFrom: Feasting at Home, Country Roads, Pantry Mama
techniques.rationale: Best fit for evening-mix, morning-shape schedule. 8-12 hours unattended fermentation.

techniques.name: Envelope fold + drag shaping
techniques.sourcedFrom: The Clever Carrot, Challenger Breadware, The Perfect Loaf
techniques.rationale: Most beginner-friendly boule shaping method. Single shape (no pre-shape) is sufficient at 70% hydration.

techniques.name: Cold proof after shaping
techniques.sourcedFrom: Universal consensus across all 9 research agents
techniques.rationale: Improves flavor (acetic acid), makes scoring easier (cold dough), increases oven spring (cold-to-hot shock), and provides schedule flexibility.

techniques.name: Bake straight from fridge
techniques.sourcedFrom: Pantry Mama, Alexandra's Kitchen, The Sourdough Journey
techniques.rationale: Cold dough + hot Dutch oven = maximum oven spring. Cold dough scores cleanly.

research.strategy: 9-agent parallel research: beginner recipes, overnight proof technique, starter readiness, baking vessel alternatives, technique science, community intel, flour & ingredients, shaping & scoring, process optimization

methods.detail: 350°F (175°C), 15 min for a half-loaf only. Run filtered water over the bread and rub it all around — not soggy, just moist. For slices, use air fryer instead.
Slice and toast or air-fry at 350°F (175°C) for ~5 min. Flexible — adjust to preference.
Cut-side down on a board, room temp, same day. Freeze sliced in zip-lock for up to 1 month.
